newsitem.title: USA: ACPC to stop publishing coffee retention indicator.
newsitem.headline: ACPC to stop publishing coffee retention indicator.

text.p: Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) said Tuesday it will cease to publish its coffee retention indicator prices.
"The ACPC retention prices are not being used and they don't have any importance at this moment," said Eduardo Libreros, vice president of the Colombia Coffee Federation.
"It is possible that we could publish them again, but I cannot say when," he added. "The ACPC is trying to keep order in the supply by organizing its members to commit to a level of export targets."

The retention indictator prices were introduced in October 1993 as an instrument to control the supply of coffee into the market. At that time, there was an abundance of supply and coffee prices had fallen near the 70.00-cent a lb level on Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange (CSCE) in New York.

The arabica retention price was calculated by taking a 20-day moving average of International Coffee Organization's (ICO) composite 79, while the robusta retention prices represent a 20-day moving average of ICO robusta prices.
"We wanted a program of control of supply based on prices, but we wanted a price different than the ICOs," said Libreros.
Traders and analysts said ending the retention indicator prices would have little effect on the futures market.
"I don't think it has that great of a significance," one analyst said. "There is no necessity to have an indicator now."
Last May, ACPC agreed to a new plan to limit green coffee exports from its members to 53.5 million 60-kg bags in the year to June 1997 against 45.8 million bags in the previous 12 months.
The 14 ACPC members account for around 80 percent of the world's coffee production.
